transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doc, to be completely honest, I didn't even really want to come in, but... well, my wife kind of insisted, and honestly, she's probably right. I'm here because I just keep blowing up at people. And I mean over absolutely nothing. It's like I have zero fuse left whatsoever. 

Just yesterday, I was on one of my morning operations calls—I manage a pretty big crew, lots of moving parts, logistics, you know how it is—and one of the guys asked a totally standard question about a delivery schedule, and I just lost it. I started snapping at him, just going off on the conference line in front of everyone. And it's not just at work, either. It's happening at home with my family, too. My kids will leave a pair of shoes in the hallway or ask what's for dinner, something they've done a million times, and I just explode. I'm shouting before I even realize what I'm doing. 

And that's... that is just not me. That is not how I’ve ever handled things in my entire life. I'm usually the guy who keeps a level head when everything else is hitting the fan, you know? As a manager, you *have* to be the calm one to keep things running. But lately, it's just this constant, boiling anger right under the surface, and the slightest little thing sets me off on this massive tirade, and I just can't seem to stop it once it starts.
Do you often feel anxious or on edge before these episodes of anger?

Well, anxious... I don't know if anxious is the right word, but on edge? Yeah, absolutely on edge. It's like I'm constantly wound up tight, like a spring that's just been cranked way past where it's supposed to go. 

It's this feeling of just waiting for the other shoe to drop, you know? Like, I'm at the warehouse, right? And any time I hear a forklift beep—you know that high-pitched backup alarm they have?—or if one of the big air compressors kicks on, which happens fifty times a day, my whole body just completely tightens up. My shoulders end up practically by my ears. I stop whatever I'm doing, whatever conversation I'm in, and I start immediately looking for the exits. I start scanning the floor, trying to figure out what's about to go wrong next, what's going to fall, what's going to break, who's going to get hurt. 

And it's not just at the warehouse, either. It followed me home. The other night, the smoke alarm in the hallway did that little low-battery chirp—just one single chirp—and I practically jumped out of my skin. I was halfway down the hall before I even realized what the sound was, just totally braced for a disaster. I was sweating, my heart was hammering against my ribs like I'd just run a marathon. My wife was looking at me like I was crazy, and honestly, I felt crazy. It's exhausting, doc. It's like my brain won't turn off that... that threat radar, even when I'm just sitting in my own living room trying to watch TV. I'm just constantly scanning, constantly waiting for something terrible to happen, and I think that's why I'm snapping at people. I'm just so exhausted from being on high alert every single second of the day.
Do you find yourself avoiding certain places or situations because of this constant feeling of being on edge?

Avoiding places? No, I... I don't think so. I mean, how could I? I'm the operations manager. If I don't show up, the whole supply chain on our end basically grinds to a halt. I've got three dozen guys relying on me to set the daily quotas, approve the manifests, handle the vendor disputes... I can't exactly just hide in my office or stay home in bed because I'm feeling jumpy, you know? 

So, no, I'm not avoiding the warehouse or anything like that, even though, like I was just saying, every single time I step out onto that concrete floor and hear those compressors kick on or the loading dock doors slamming shut, my heart is right up in my throat. I just... I force myself to walk out there anyway. I'll grip my clipboard so hard my knuckles turn white, and I just push through it. My wife, bless her, she keeps telling me, "Take a sick day, take a week off, just go sit in the quiet somewhere," but she doesn't really get how the industry works. You don't just walk away from a logistics hub when you're the one steering the ship. 

So I'm there. Every single morning at 6 AM, I am pulling my truck into that parking lot. I don't avoid the floor, I don't avoid the morning stand-up meetings, I don't avoid the breakroom... I just sit there and endure it. I mean, maybe I wish I could avoid it all, sure, but in reality? No. I'm just white-knuckling my way through every single day, everywhere I go, just waiting for the shift to end so I can go home and be on edge there instead.
Do you experience any physical symptoms like headaches or tremors when you're feeling on edge?

Headaches... no, not really. I mean, I've never been a headache guy to begin with. Some of the guys on the dock, they complain about migraines or tension headaches all the time, especially with the fluorescent lights in the main office or the constant noise from the machinery, but I've always had a pretty thick skull, I guess. Even with all this... whatever this is lately, my head itself doesn't hurt. 

And as for tremors, like shaking? No, I don't have that either. My hands are steady. Like I said before, I grip my clipboard so tight my knuckles go white, so it's more like my muscles are just locked up solid, rather than shaking. If I was standing there trembling, the crew would definitely notice, and you just can't have that in my position. You can't be the guy in charge and look like you're vibrating out of your boots on the warehouse floor, you know? They'd lose all confidence in me, or they'd think I was going through withdrawals or something crazy like that. 

So, no, no shaking. It's just that intense tightness, the shoulders creeping all the way up to my ears, and my heart hammering away like I told you about when that smoke detector went off. But actual pain in my head or my hands physically shaking? No, I haven't noticed anything like that at all. I guess I'm just completely rigid instead of shaky. It's all just locked in tight.
Do you ever feel like you're outside of your body watching yourself when you're in these intense situations?

Outside of my body? Like... like watching myself from above or something? No, no, definitely not. I mean, I've heard people talk about that kind of thing, you know, on TV shows or whatever, when they go through something crazy and they say it felt like a movie. But for me? No, I am very, very much in my body. 

If anything, I feel like I'm trapped in it even more than usual. Like I was saying before about the tightness and the heart pounding... I feel every single bit of that. When I'm out on the floor and the forklift backs up, or the compressor kicks on, I don't feel disconnected at all. I feel every muscle clamping down. I feel the sweat starting on the back of my neck. I feel my boots on the concrete and I feel exactly how hard I'm squeezing that clipboard. 

It's actually the opposite of feeling outside myself, I think. It's like I'm hyper-aware of every physical sensation, every breath I take, every time my heart slams into my ribs. Like with the smoke detector at home—when that chirped, I didn't float away. I was instantly, intensely aware that I was moving down the hallway, that my breathing was shallow, that I was sweating. I felt all of it, maybe too much of it. So, no, I've never had that feeling of watching myself. I'm right there, in the thick of it, feeling every single miserable second of being locked up and on edge.
Do you ever feel numb or disconnected from your emotions when you're not in one of these intense situations?

Numb? Disconnected... I mean, yeah, I guess you could say that. But it's not like I'm walking around like a zombie or something. It's more about... well, it's about the good stuff, I suppose. It's like... I don't know, it's like the part of me that's supposed to feel happy or relaxed is just broken right now, or turned off. 

Like, take the other night, for example. I finally get home, right? It's been a 12-hour day, I'm exhausted, I'm wound tight as a drum. I walk in the door, and my wife, she's made this great dinner—meatloaf, mashed potatoes, the works. It's my favorite, she knows it's my favorite. She's trying so hard to make things nice, to give me a break. And the kids are at the table, and they're going on and on about their soccer practice, who scored what, who tripped over the ball, just normal kid stuff. The kind of stuff that usually, you know, it makes you smile. It makes you feel good to be a dad, to be home, to have this family. 

But I'm sitting there, looking at my plate, listening to them chatter, and... nothing. I mean, I know in my head that I should be happy. I know I should feel glad to be sitting there with my family, safe in my own house, eating a hot meal. I can look at the situation and say, "This is good. You are a lucky guy." But inside? It's just... flat. Empty. It's like there's nothing in me that can respond to them anymore. I can't muster up a smile that doesn't feel completely fake. I can't feel that warmth, that joy, whatever you want to call it. 

It's just this heavy, blank feeling. And the worst part is, I know they see it. My wife gives me this look, this sad, worried look, because she knows I'm a million miles away, even though I'm sitting right next to her. And I want to tell her, "Hey, it's great, I love it, I'm so happy to be here," but the words would just be dust in my mouth. Because I don't feel it. I just don't feel any of the good stuff at all right now. It's like all my energy is going into just keeping my grip on that clipboard and not jumping out of my skin, and there's just zero juice left over for anything positive.
Have you experienced any particularly traumatic or stressful events recently or in your past?

Traumatic? Yeah. Yeah, I have. That's... that's why I'm here, really. It's why I've been a wreck for the last three weeks. Exactly three weeks this Thursday, actually. 

We had a massive valve failure on the main line at the facility. I manage the whole floor, you know? I've been there fifteen years, worked my way up, I know every inch of that warehouse. I know the sounds the machines are supposed to make. And that morning, the pressure gauge on the main compressor line was acting up, but maintenance said they had it handled. They said they bled the line. 

I was standing maybe twenty feet away, talking to one of my shift supervisors, Dave. Good guy, Dave. We were just going over the shipping manifest for the afternoon, totally routine. And then... the sound. I can't even describe the sound. It wasn't just loud, it was like the air got sucked out of the room and then exploded back in. The main valve just blew. Completely sheared off. 

A piece of the housing, heavy steel, it shot across the floor like a cannonball. It hit one of my guys, Marcus. He was just walking back from the break room. Just walking back with a cup of coffee. It took his leg right out from under him. The blood... I've never seen so much blood in my life. It was everywhere. And the noise from the pipe, the air screaming out of it, it was deafening, you couldn't even hear Marcus screaming at first. 

I had to run over there, I had to grab my belt and use it as a tourniquet while Dave called 911. My hands were covered in it. I was kneeling in it. I kept telling him he was going to be okay, but his face was so gray, and his eyes were rolling back. I thought he was going to die right there on the concrete, right under my hands. 

He lived, thank God. They managed to save the leg, barely, but he's got a long road ahead. But ever since that day... three weeks ago... I can't get the sound out of my head. I can't get the smell of the copper and the oil out of my nose. Every time I walk past that spot on the floor, my chest seizes up. Every time a forklift drops a pallet a little too hard, I'm right back there, kneeling in it. So yeah, that... that was the event. That's what started all this. Three weeks of this absolute hell.
Do you find yourself avoiding the specific area of the warehouse where the valve failure occurred?

Avoid it? Man, I wish I could. I really, really wish I could just tape off that whole section of the warehouse and never step foot in it again. But I can't. I'm the operations manager, you know? That main compressor line is right in the middle of our primary staging area for outbound freight. It's the main artery of the whole floor. There is literally no way for me to do my job and avoid that spot. 

I mean, I guess I could just hide out in the glass office upstairs and watch the floor from the catwalk, but that's not how I run things. I've been there fifteen years because I'm actually on the floor with my guys. I have to be down there to check the manifests, check the safety protocols, make sure the pallets are wrapped right and loaded on time. 

So, no, I don't avoid it. I walk past that exact spot... God, maybe ten, twelve times a shift. And it's exactly where Marcus went down. They brought in a hazmat crew to scrub the concrete, they power-washed that whole aisle, but I swear to you, I know exactly which expansion joint he was lying next to. I can still see it in my head perfectly. And Dave—my shift supervisor, I mentioned Dave earlier—he's been great, he actually offered to run the shipping slips back and forth for me so I wouldn't have to go down to that end of the building. But I told him no. I have to do my job. I can't let my crew see me hiding.

But every single time I have to walk down that aisle, it's just... it's an absolute nightmare. Like I said before about my chest seizing up? It happens every single time I get within fifty feet of that new valve housing. I'm walking, and I'm trying to look at the inventory tags, trying to focus on the forklift traffic, but my whole body is just bracing for an explosion. I'm gripping my clipboard so hard my hands cramp up, and I'm just waiting for that deafening pop, waiting for the screaming to start all over again. I force myself to walk right through it, right past the spot, but it drains every ounce of energy out of me. By the time I get back to the office, I'm drenched in sweat and my heart is going a million miles an hour. So I definitely don't avoid it, I'm right there in it. It's just taking a massive toll on me having to force myself through it every single day.

Every time a forklift drops a pallet a little too hard, I'm right back there, kneeling in it. So yeah, that... that was the event. That's what started all this. Three weeks of this absolute hell.

Avoid it? Man, I wish I could. I really, really wish I could just tape off that whole section of the warehouse and never step foot in it again. But I can't. I'm the operations manager, you know? That main compressor line is right in the middle of our primary staging area for outbound freight. It's the main artery of the whole floor. There is literally no way for me to do my job and avoid that spot. 

I mean, I guess I could just hide out in the glass office upstairs and watch the floor from the catwalk, but that's not how I run things. I've been there fifteen years because I'm actually on the floor with my guys. I have to be down there to check the manifests, check the safety protocols, make sure the pallets are wrapped right and loaded on time. 

So, no, I don't avoid it. I walk past that exact spot... God, maybe ten, twelve times a shift. And it's exactly where Marcus went down. They brought in a hazmat crew to scrub the concrete, they power-washed that whole aisle, but I swear to you, I know exactly which expansion joint he was lying next to. I can still see it in my head perfectly. And Dave—my shift supervisor, I mentioned Dave earlier—he's been great, he actually offered to run the shipping slips back and forth for me so I wouldn't have to go down to that end of the building. But I told him no. I have to do my job. I can't let my crew see me hiding.

But every single time I have to walk down that aisle, it's just... it's an absolute nightmare. Like I said before about my chest seizing up? It happens every single time I get within fifty feet of that new valve housing. I'm walking, and I'm trying to look at the inventory tags, trying to focus on the forklift traffic, but my whole body is just bracing for an explosion. I'm gripping my clipboard so hard my hands cramp up, and I'm just waiting for that deafening pop, waiting for the screaming to start all over again. I force myself to walk right through it, right past the spot, but it drains every ounce of energy out of me. By the time I get back to the office, I'm drenched in sweat and my heart is going a million miles an hour. So I definitely don't avoid it, I'm right there in it. It's just taking a massive toll on me having to force myself through it every single day.
